q: What are IAM permissions boundaries, and how are they different from SCPs and session policies?
p: A permissions boundary is a managed policy that sets the maximum permissions an IAM user or role can ever have. Effective permissions are the intersection of the identity policy and the boundary. SCPs do the same at account level and session policies at session level.
tip: The classic use is delegated administration: let teams create roles, but only roles that carry the boundary.
a: A permissions boundary is a managed policy attached to a user or role that defines the ceiling of what that identity can do. It never grants anything by itself. The effective permission is the intersection of the identity policy and the boundary, so even an administrator policy cannot exceed it. Service control policies work the same way but at the account or organizational unit level, and session policies limit a single assumed-role session. I use boundaries for delegated administration: platform teams let developers create their own roles, but only if the new role carries a required boundary, enforced with a condition on iam:PermissionsBoundary in the developer's policy. That prevents privilege escalation through self-created admin roles. When debugging an unexpected access denied, I check all layers: SCP, boundary, session policy, identity policy and resource policy, because an explicit deny or a missing allow in any of them blocks the call.

q: Why use IAM Identity Center (SSO) instead of IAM users for people, and how do permission sets work?
p: Identity Center gives people short-lived credentials via your identity provider, one login across accounts, and central assignment. A permission set is a template that is turned into an IAM role in each assigned account.
tip: Say that long-lived IAM user access keys for humans are the first thing a security review flags.
a: IAM users carry long-lived passwords and access keys that leak, are shared and are hard to offboard across many accounts. IAM Identity Center connects to the company identity provider, such as Okta or Entra ID, so people sign in once with their normal credentials and multi-factor authentication, then pick an account and role. They receive short-lived credentials that expire automatically. Administrators define permission sets, which are reusable bundles of policies, and assign a group to a permission set in specific accounts. Behind the scenes, Identity Center creates an IAM role in each target account. Offboarding becomes one action in the identity provider, and CloudTrail shows who really did what. For workloads I do not use users at all, I use roles. I keep one break-glass IAM user or role, with hardware MFA and alerts, in case the identity provider is down.

q: How do you use IAM Access Analyzer to reach least privilege?
p: Access Analyzer finds resources shared outside your zone of trust, flags unused access and permissions, and can generate a least-privilege policy from CloudTrail activity. Policy validation catches errors before deploy.
tip: Start broad in dev, then tighten using generated policies from real usage, rather than guessing in advance.
a: Access Analyzer helps in three ways. External access findings show S3 buckets, roles, KMS keys, queues and other resources that can be reached from outside the account or organization, so I can find accidental public or cross-account exposure. Unused access findings show roles, users and permissions that have not been used for a defined period, which lets me remove stale access. Policy generation reads CloudTrail logs for a role over a period, often ninety days, and drafts a policy that only includes the actions actually used. I review it, replace wildcards on resources where possible and attach it. Policy validation and custom checks in the pipeline catch problems like overly broad actions or missing conditions before they reach production. My workflow is to begin with a reasonably scoped policy, observe real usage, then tighten, and repeat on a schedule.
f: What are the limits of CloudTrail-based policy generation?
How do you handle rarely used permissions such as disaster recovery?

q: Gateway versus interface VPC endpoints: what is the difference and when do you use each?
p: Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB, are free, and work through route table entries. Interface endpoints use PrivateLink, create ENIs with private IPs in your subnets, cost per hour and per GB, and support many services.
cmds: aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-id vpc-1 --service-name com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.s3 --route-table-ids rtb-1
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-endpoint-type Interface --service-name com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.ecr.api --subnet-ids subnet-1 --security-group-ids sg-1
tip: Adding an S3 gateway endpoint is the quickest cut to NAT Gateway data charges.
a: Both let private subnets reach AWS services without going over the internet or a NAT Gateway. A gateway endpoint is a target in the route table, available only for S3 and DynamoDB, and it has no hourly or data charge. An interface endpoint is built on PrivateLink: it creates elastic network interfaces with private IPs in your subnets, uses security groups, supports private DNS, and works for most other services such as ECR, STS, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch and SQS. It has an hourly cost per availability zone and a per-gigabyte charge. In practice I add the S3 gateway endpoint to every VPC, because it reduces NAT costs, and add interface endpoints for services that private workloads use heavily, such as ECR and logs for EKS nodes. I use endpoint policies to restrict which buckets or actions can be reached, and deploy interface endpoints in each zone the workloads run in.

q: Site-to-Site VPN versus Direct Connect: how do you choose and design for resilience?
p: VPN is quick to set up, encrypted over the internet, and limited to about 1.25 Gbps per tunnel with variable latency. Direct Connect is a private dedicated link with consistent latency and higher bandwidth, but takes weeks and is not encrypted by default.
tip: The usual answer: Direct Connect as primary, VPN as backup, and MACsec or VPN over Direct Connect if encryption is required.
a: A Site-to-Site VPN creates IPsec tunnels over the public internet. It is fast to set up, cheap and encrypted, but each tunnel is limited in throughput and latency can vary. Direct Connect provides a dedicated private connection from your data center or colocation facility, with predictable latency, higher bandwidth and lower data transfer charges, but lead times are longer and traffic is not encrypted unless you add MACsec or run a VPN over it. For resilience I never rely on a single link. A common design is two Direct Connect connections at different locations as primary, with a VPN as a backup path, all advertised through BGP with proper preference settings, terminating on a Transit Gateway or Direct Connect Gateway. I test failover regularly and monitor BGP session state and tunnel status with alarms.
f: How do you prefer one path over another with BGP?

q: How does Route 53 Resolver work for hybrid DNS between AWS and on-premises?
p: The VPC resolver at the base of the VPC CIDR plus 2 answers queries. Inbound endpoints let on-prem DNS query AWS private zones. Outbound endpoints with forwarding rules send chosen domains to on-prem DNS servers.
cmds: aws route53resolver create-resolver-endpoint --direction INBOUND --security-group-ids sg-1 --ip-addresses SubnetId=subnet-1 SubnetId=subnet-2
aws route53resolver create-resolver-rule --rule-type FORWARD --domain-name corp.example.com --target-ips Ip=10.1.0.2
tip: Put at least two IPs in different zones on each endpoint and share forwarding rules through AWS RAM.
a: Each VPC has a built-in DNS resolver that handles public names and private hosted zones. For hybrid setups, you need a way to cross the boundary. An inbound resolver endpoint gives on-premises DNS servers IP addresses inside the VPC to forward queries to, so they can resolve private hosted zone records and internal names. An outbound endpoint lets the VPC resolver forward queries for specific domains, such as corp.example.com, to on-premises DNS servers, using forwarding rules. Rules can be shared across accounts and associated with many VPCs using Resource Access Manager, which suits a multi-account landing zone. For reliability I place endpoint IPs in at least two availability zones, secure them with security groups, and monitor query volume. I also keep a clear ownership model for which domains are resolved where, to avoid loops.

q: What are EC2 placement groups, and when would you use cluster, spread or partition?
p: Cluster packs instances close together in one zone for low latency and high throughput. Spread puts each instance on distinct hardware, up to 7 per zone. Partition groups instances into racks that do not share hardware, for large distributed systems.
tip: Cluster groups can fail with insufficient capacity, so launch all instances at once and use a single instance type.
a: Placement groups influence where instances run on the underlying hardware. A cluster group places instances close together in a single availability zone, giving the lowest latency and highest network throughput, which suits HPC, tightly coupled jobs and some distributed training. The risk is a shared failure domain and capacity errors, so I launch the whole group at once. A spread group places each instance on separate racks, limited to seven running instances per zone, which is right for a small number of critical instances that must not fail together, such as primary and standby. A partition group divides instances into logical partitions on separate racks, which fits large, rack-aware systems like Kafka, Cassandra or HDFS, where the application knows partition boundaries. I choose based on whether latency or fault isolation matters more, and check capacity before relying on them.

q: When does Lambda cost more than containers, and how do you decide between them?
p: Lambda charges per request and per GB-second, so it is cheap for spiky or idle workloads and expensive for steady high-volume traffic. Containers on Fargate or EC2 are cheaper at constant utilisation, but you manage scaling and idle capacity.
tip: Do a break-even calculation with real request rate, duration and memory rather than choosing by fashion.
a: Lambda bills for requests and for memory multiplied by duration, with no cost when idle, so it is excellent for spiky, unpredictable or low-volume work, event-driven glue and workloads that scale to zero. As traffic becomes steady and high, paying per millisecond costs more than running containers at good utilisation. Other factors also matter: Lambda has time limits, cold starts, concurrency limits and a package size ceiling, while containers handle long-running processes, websockets and special runtimes more naturally. I compare with a simple model: requests per second, average duration and memory for Lambda, versus the number of tasks needed and their utilisation for Fargate or EC2. I also include operational cost, because Lambda removes much patching and scaling work. Many systems use both, with Lambda for events and containers for the steady core API.

q: How do Auto Scaling warm pools and instance refresh help with deployments and scale-out speed?
p: A warm pool keeps pre-initialised stopped or running instances ready, so scale-out skips long boot and bootstrap time. Instance refresh replaces instances in an ASG gradually when the launch template or AMI changes, with a minimum healthy percentage.
tip: Use lifecycle hooks so warm instances finish their setup before they enter service.
a: When an application takes minutes to boot, install packages or warm caches, scaling out in response to load is too slow. A warm pool keeps a set of pre-initialised instances on the side, either stopped, which costs only storage, or running, so that when the group needs capacity it takes from the pool and the instances reach service much sooner. Lifecycle hooks let you run initialisation before an instance joins and cleanup before it leaves. Instance refresh handles rollouts: when you update the launch template, AMI or instance type, it replaces instances in batches, keeping a minimum healthy percentage and waiting for a warmup period, with automatic rollback on alarms if configured. I combine this with baked AMIs to reduce boot time, health checks tied to the load balancer, and checkpoints so I can pause a rollout if error rates rise.
f: Stopped versus running warm pool: which is cheaper?

q: Managed node groups, self-managed nodes, Fargate and Karpenter on EKS: how do you choose?
p: Managed node groups automate provisioning and rolling updates of EC2 workers. Self-managed gives full control over the AMI and bootstrap. Fargate runs each pod in its own microVM with no nodes to manage. Karpenter provisions right-sized nodes on demand.
cmds: aws eks create-nodegroup --cluster-name prod --nodegroup-name ng-1 --subnets subnet-1 subnet-2 --node-role <arn>
tip: A common production answer is managed node groups or Karpenter for general workloads, plus Fargate for small isolated jobs.
a: Managed node groups let EKS create and update the Auto Scaling group, drain nodes during updates and keep AMIs patched, so they are a safe default. Self-managed nodes make sense when you need a custom AMI, special kernel settings or unusual bootstrap logic, but you own the lifecycle. Fargate removes nodes entirely and bills per pod resources, which is good for isolated or bursty workloads, but it lacks DaemonSets, privileged pods and GPUs, and has higher cost per unit. Karpenter watches pending pods and launches nodes of the right size and type, including Spot, then consolidates and removes underused nodes, giving better packing than fixed node groups. My usual design is a small managed node group for system components and Karpenter for application capacity, with Fargate only where per-pod isolation is valuable.

How does Karpenter consolidation work?

q: EKS Pod Identity versus IRSA: how do they give pods AWS permissions, and which is better?
p: IRSA uses the cluster's OIDC provider and a service account annotation, with a trust policy per cluster. EKS Pod Identity uses an agent and an association between a service account and a role, with one reusable trust policy and no OIDC setup per cluster.
cmds: aws eks create-pod-identity-association --cluster-name prod --namespace app --service-account web --role-arn <arn>
kubectl annotate sa web eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn=<arn>  # IRSA
tip: Mention that both avoid node-wide instance profile permissions, which every pod on the node would share.
a: Both remove the need for static keys and for broad node instance roles. With IRSA, the cluster has an OIDC identity provider. A Kubernetes service account is annotated with a role ARN, and the role's trust policy allows web identity tokens from that provider for a specific namespace and service account. The SDK exchanges the projected token for temporary credentials. It works well but needs an OIDC provider and a separately edited trust policy for every cluster. EKS Pod Identity moves this into an EKS feature: a DaemonSet agent serves credentials, and you create an association between cluster, namespace, service account and role. The role trusts the EKS pods service principal, and the same role can be reused across clusters. Pod Identity is simpler to operate and adds session tags. I choose it for new clusters, and keep IRSA where older SDK versions or Fargate constraints require it.

q: How do ECS task definitions, services and task roles fit together, and what is the difference between the execution role and the task role?
p: A task definition describes containers, CPU, memory and roles. A service keeps a desired number of tasks running behind a load balancer. The execution role lets ECS pull images and write logs; the task role is what your application code uses to call AWS APIs.
cmds: aws ecs update-service --cluster prod --service web --task-definition web:42 --force-new-deployment
tip: Mixing the two roles up is the most common ECS permissions bug in interviews and in production.
a: A task definition is the blueprint: container images, ports, CPU and memory, environment, logging and IAM roles. A task is one running instance of it. A service ensures a desired count of tasks, replaces failed ones, integrates with a load balancer and performs rolling or blue-green deployments. There are two roles that people mix up. The task execution role belongs to the ECS agent, and grants permission to pull images from ECR, fetch secrets for injection and send logs to CloudWatch. The task role is assumed by your application code inside the container, so it carries permissions for S3, DynamoDB or SQS. Following least privilege means giving each service its own task role. If a container starts but the app gets access denied, I check the task role. If the task never starts or cannot pull its image, I check the execution role and network path.

q: Compare EBS gp3, io2 and st1 volumes, and explain how snapshots work.
p: gp3 is general-purpose SSD with baseline 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s that you can raise independently. io2 provides provisioned, high-durability IOPS for databases. st1 is throughput-optimised HDD for large sequential workloads. Snapshots are incremental and stored in S3.
tip: Moving gp2 to gp3 online is a free cost and performance win, which interviewers like to hear.
a: gp3 is the default choice. It gives a baseline of three thousand IOPS and one hundred twenty-five megabytes per second regardless of size, and lets you raise IOPS and throughput separately, at a lower price than gp2. io2 and io2 Block Express offer provisioned IOPS up to very high levels, sub-millisecond latency and higher durability, suited to critical databases. st1 and sc1 are magnetic volumes for big sequential workloads like logs or data warehouses and cannot be boot volumes. Snapshots are point-in-time backups stored in S3, and after the first full copy they are incremental, so only changed blocks are saved. A snapshot is crash-consistent, so for databases I quiesce or use application-aware tooling. Volumes can be modified online, so I migrate gp2 to gp3 without downtime, and automate backups with Data Lifecycle Manager or AWS Backup, plus restore tests.

q: What are S3 presigned URLs, and how do you use them securely for uploads and downloads?
p: A presigned URL embeds temporary credentials and a signature so a client can GET or PUT one object without AWS credentials. It inherits the permissions of whoever signed it and expires after the time you set.
tip: Keep expiry short, pin the key and content type, and remember the URL is a bearer token: anyone who has it can use it.
a: A presigned URL lets a user or app perform a specific S3 operation on a specific object for a limited time without having AWS credentials. The URL carries a signature created by an IAM principal, and S3 evaluates the request with that principal's permissions, so if the signer loses access, or if temporary credentials used to sign expire first, the URL stops working. I use them so browsers upload large files directly to S3 and skip my servers, and to serve private downloads. To use them securely I set short expiries, generate the key server-side so users cannot choose it, restrict content type and size using presigned POST conditions, keep the bucket private with Block Public Access, and log access. Because anyone holding the link can use it, I avoid putting sensitive links in places that get logged or shared, and consider CloudFront signed URLs for broader distribution.

q: EFS performance and throughput modes: how do you pick and avoid surprises?
p: EFS is elastic NFS storage. Throughput modes are Elastic, Provisioned and Bursting; performance mode is General Purpose for almost all workloads. Metadata-heavy small-file patterns and cross-AZ mounts are the usual sources of slowness.
tip: Mount using the mount target in the same availability zone as the client to avoid cross-AZ latency and charges.
a: EFS provides shared, elastic NFS storage across many instances and zones. Performance mode should almost always be General Purpose, since Max I/O is a legacy option. Throughput mode matters more. Elastic automatically scales throughput with the workload and is the best default when demand is unpredictable. Provisioned lets you pay for a fixed throughput regardless of size, useful when you know the need. Bursting ties throughput to the amount of data stored, which can starve small file systems. EFS performs well for large sequential access and shared content, but small files and heavy metadata operations have higher latency than local disk. I mount through the target in the same zone, use TLS and IAM authorisation, use access points to enforce paths and identities for containers, apply lifecycle policies to move cold data to Infrequent Access, and avoid it for latency-sensitive databases.

q: RDS Multi-AZ versus read replicas: what does each give you, and do they replace each other?
p: Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby for high availability and automatic failover, and you cannot read from the classic standby. Read replicas use asynchronous replication to scale reads and can be cross-region. They solve different problems.
tip: Add that replica lag means reads can be stale, so read-your-own-writes paths must use the primary.
a: Multi-AZ is about availability. RDS maintains a standby in another zone with synchronous replication, and if the primary fails, or during maintenance, it promotes the standby and flips the DNS endpoint, usually within a minute or two. In the classic single-standby setup you cannot read from the standby, although the newer Multi-AZ cluster option provides two readable standbys. Read replicas are about scale and distance. They use asynchronous replication, so they can lag, and you point read traffic at their endpoints. They can also be placed in other regions and can be promoted for disaster recovery, but promotion is manual and loses unreplicated writes. So they do not replace each other. A typical production design uses Multi-AZ for the primary and one or more replicas for read-heavy reporting. My application must handle reconnects after failover and tolerate replica lag.

What does Aurora do differently?

q: How do DynamoDB Streams and TTL work, and what are they used for?
p: Streams capture an ordered 24-hour log of item changes, which Lambda or Kinesis consumers can process. TTL deletes expired items for free in the background, within a day or two of expiry, and the deletions also appear in the stream.
tip: TTL is not exact: expired items can stay readable, so filter on the timestamp in queries.
a: DynamoDB Streams records item-level changes, inserts, updates and deletes, in order per item, and keeps them for twenty-four hours. You choose what each record contains: keys only, new image, old image, or both. A Lambda function is typically subscribed to react to changes, for example to update a search index, send notifications, maintain aggregates or replicate to another store. Processing must be idempotent because records may be delivered more than once. TTL lets you mark an attribute holding an epoch timestamp, and DynamoDB deletes expired items in the background at no write cost, which suits sessions, tokens and temporary data. Deletion can lag by up to a couple of days, so queries should filter expired items explicitly. TTL deletes show up in the stream with a service identity, so consumers can distinguish them from user deletions.

q: What does RDS Proxy do, and when is it worth using?
p: RDS Proxy pools and shares database connections, reduces failover time by holding connections, and can use IAM auth with Secrets Manager credentials. It is most useful with Lambda or apps that open many short connections.
cmds: aws rds create-db-proxy --db-proxy-name app-proxy --engine-family POSTGRESQL --auth AuthScheme=SECRETS,SecretArn=<arn> --role-arn <arn> --vpc-subnet-ids subnet-1 subnet-2
tip: Watch for session pinning, because pinned connections cannot be shared and reduce the benefit.
a: RDS Proxy sits between the application and an RDS or Aurora database. It maintains a pool of established connections and multiplexes many client connections onto fewer database connections, which protects the database from connection storms. That is common with Lambda, where each concurrent invocation could open its own connection and exhaust the max connections limit. The proxy also shortens failover impact, because it keeps client connections and reconnects to the new primary on the backend, and it supports IAM authentication and credentials stored in Secrets Manager, so apps do not embed passwords. There are costs and caveats: it adds a small latency hop and a per-vCPU charge, and features like session variables, temporary tables or prepared statements can cause session pinning, which reduces multiplexing. I use it for serverless or bursty workloads, and for a stable pool with PgBouncer or an application pool I may not need it.

q: How do you use CloudWatch Logs Insights to investigate an incident quickly?
p: Logs Insights runs a purpose-built query language over log groups. You filter, parse fields, aggregate and chart. Structured JSON logs make fields queryable immediately, so you can find error spikes, top offenders and slow requests in seconds.
cmds: fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /ERROR/ | stats count() by bin(5m)
filter status >= 500 | stats count() as c by path | sort c desc | limit 10
fields @timestamp, duration | stats pct(duration, 99) by bin(1m)
tip: Query cost is per GB scanned, so narrow the time range and log groups first.
a: Logs Insights lets me query one or many log groups interactively. A typical incident flow is to pick the affected log groups and a tight time window around the start of the problem, then count errors per five-minute bin to find when it began. Next I group by dimensions such as path, status code, host or customer ID to see whether it is isolated. Then I look at percentile latency over time and sample the raw error messages. If logs are structured JSON, fields like level, requestId and duration are automatically discovered, which makes the queries short, otherwise I use parse with a pattern. I save common queries, add them to dashboards, and create metric filters for the patterns I want to alert on. Since I pay for data scanned, I scope queries carefully, and for long-term analytics I export logs to S3 and use Athena.

q: What does CloudWatch Container Insights give you for ECS and EKS, and what are its limits?
p: Container Insights collects cluster, node, pod and task level CPU, memory, network and storage metrics and performance logs, with prebuilt dashboards. It is easy to enable but can be expensive at scale and is less flexible than Prometheus.
tip: Point out the cost lever: metrics and logs are charged per metric and per GB, so review which are enabled.
a: Container Insights provides managed collection of container metrics without running your own monitoring stack. For EKS you install the CloudWatch observability add-on, which deploys the agent and Fluent Bit, and for ECS you enable it on the cluster. You get metrics for clusters, nodes, services, pods and tasks, such as CPU, memory, network, restarts and storage, performance log events with high-cardinality data, and curated dashboards plus support for application signals and trace links. It is quick to adopt and integrates with alarms, anomaly detection and X-Ray. The limits are cost, since every metric and log GB is billed, and flexibility, because PromQL, custom exporters and open-source ecosystem dashboards are not available. Many teams combine it for baseline infrastructure signals with Amazon Managed Prometheus and Grafana for application metrics and richer queries.

q: What are CloudWatch composite alarms and anomaly detection, and how do they cut alert noise?
p: A composite alarm combines other alarms with AND, OR and NOT rules so you page only when several symptoms agree. Anomaly detection learns the normal band for a metric, accounting for time-of-day patterns, and alarms outside that band.
cmds: aws cloudwatch put-composite-alarm --alarm-name checkout-down --alarm-rule "ALARM(high-5xx) AND ALARM(low-orders)"
aws cloudwatch put-anomaly-detector --namespace AWS/ApplicationELB --metric-name RequestCount --stat Sum
tip: Alert on user-facing symptoms and use the cause alarms as suppressed inputs or dashboards.
a: A single metric threshold is often noisy. A composite alarm evaluates the state of other alarms using a boolean expression, so I can page only when, for example, the error rate is high and order volume is low, rather than whenever CPU briefly spikes. It can also suppress child notifications, so on-call receives one alert for the incident instead of twenty. Anomaly detection uses a machine learning model trained on history to create an expected band, adapting to hourly, daily and weekly patterns, so I can alarm when traffic or latency falls outside normal without choosing a static number. It is good for seasonal metrics, but I check the band is sensible and exclude past incidents from training. In general, I alert on symptoms customers feel, keep cause-level alarms for investigation, and review noisy alerts monthly.

q: Compute Savings Plans versus EC2 Instance Savings Plans versus Reserved Instances: how do you choose and avoid over-commitment?
p: Compute Savings Plans commit to a dollar-per-hour spend and apply across EC2, Fargate and Lambda in any region and family. EC2 Instance plans give a deeper discount for one family in one region. Reserved Instances are tied to specific instance attributes.
cmds: aws ce get-savings-plans-purchase-recommendation --savings-plans-type COMPUTE_SP --term-in-years ONE_YEAR --payment-option NO_UPFRONT --lookback-period-in-days THIRTY_DAYS
tip: Commit to your stable baseline, around 60 to 70 percent, never to peak usage.
a: All of these trade a one or three year commitment for lower prices. A Compute Savings Plan commits to spending a certain dollar amount per hour and automatically applies to EC2 regardless of family, size, region or operating system, and also to Fargate and Lambda, so it is the most flexible. An EC2 Instance Savings Plan gives a larger discount but is locked to a family in a region. Reserved Instances apply to specific instance attributes and can be sold or converted in some cases, and they are still used for RDS, ElastiCache and OpenSearch, which have their own reservations. I analyse the baseline using Cost Explorer's recommendations, commit only to the steady portion, stagger purchases through the year so expiry is smooth, and track coverage and utilisation. If I plan a migration to Graviton or containers, the flexible plan is safer.

How do you stagger commitments?

q: How do you use Compute Optimizer and rightsizing recommendations without hurting performance?
p: Compute Optimizer analyses CloudWatch utilisation, usually 14 days, and recommends smaller or different instance types, EBS volumes, Lambda memory and ECS on Fargate sizes. Validate against peak, memory metrics and business cycles before acting.
tip: Memory is not collected by default, so install the CloudWatch agent or the recommendation misses the key signal.
a: Compute Optimizer looks at utilisation history from CloudWatch and suggests a better fit: whether an instance is over-provisioned, under-provisioned or optimised, and which types would perform better or cost less. It also covers EBS volumes, Lambda memory settings, Auto Scaling groups and Fargate. To use it safely, I first make sure the right data is present, particularly memory through the CloudWatch agent and a long enough lookback, including month-end or seasonal peaks. Then I rank by savings and risk, test changes in a lower environment or on a canary instance, and apply them gradually using infrastructure as code. I confirm latency and error rates after each change and keep the previous size for easy rollback. Graviton options often show up as additional savings. I treat the tool as input to a decision, not an automatic instruction.
f: Why isn't CPU alone enough?
How do you roll back a rightsizing change?

q: How do you design a tagging strategy that really supports cost allocation?
p: Define a small mandatory set such as owner, team, environment, cost-center and application. Activate them as cost allocation tags, enforce with tag policies, SCPs and IaC checks, and handle untaggable spend with account structure and shared-cost rules.
cmds: aws organizations create-policy --type TAG_POLICY --name std-tags --content file://tags.json
tip: Tags only apply from activation onward, so activate early. Tag policies check values but do not stop untagged resources by themselves.
a: A good strategy starts small and enforceable. I choose a handful of mandatory tags, such as team, owner, environment, application and cost center, with allowed values. In AWS Billing I activate them as cost allocation tags, because they do not appear in reports until activated and are not retroactive. Enforcement happens at several layers: tag policies in Organizations standardise keys and values, service control policies or IAM conditions can deny creation without required tags, and Terraform or CloudFormation modules apply default tags and pipeline checks fail untagged resources. Not everything can be tagged or attributed, so I use a separate account per team or environment as the strongest boundary, and allocate shared costs like networking proportionally. Then I build showback dashboards and review untagged spend weekly, so the tags remain accurate over time.
f: Why are accounts a stronger boundary than tags?
How do you handle shared platform costs?

q: How do you let GitHub Actions or another CI system deploy to AWS without static access keys?
p: Use OpenID Connect federation. Create an IAM OIDC identity provider for the CI issuer, then a role whose trust policy allows web identity from that provider with conditions on repository and branch. The job exchanges its token for temporary credentials.
tip: Always constrain the sub claim to a specific repo and branch or environment. A trust policy that accepts any repository is a real vulnerability.
a: Instead of storing an access key in CI secrets, I establish trust between AWS and the CI provider. In IAM I create an OpenID Connect identity provider for the provider's token issuer. Then I create a deployment role whose trust policy allows sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity from that provider, with conditions on the audience and on the subject claim so only a particular repository, branch, tag or environment can assume it. During the pipeline run, the CI platform issues a short-lived signed token, the job exchanges it for temporary credentials that expire in about an hour, and no long-lived secret exists to leak or rotate. I give each role least-privilege permissions for its job, separate roles for plan and apply, and for production require a protected environment with approval. I also log role assumptions in CloudTrail and alert on unexpected subjects.
f: What does the sub claim contain?
How would you separate plan and apply permissions?

q: How do ECS blue/green deployments with CodeDeploy work?
p: CodeDeploy launches a new task set behind a second target group, shifts the ALB listener traffic all at once, linearly or as a canary, runs lifecycle hook tests, and can roll back automatically on alarms. The old task set is kept briefly for fast rollback.
cmds: aws deploy create-deployment --application-name web --deployment-group-name prod --revision file://appspec.json
tip: Use a test listener port and a BeforeAllowTraffic hook to smoke test before real users see the new version.
a: With the CodeDeploy deployment controller, an ECS service has two target groups on the load balancer. When a deployment starts, CodeDeploy creates a replacement task set running the new task definition and registers it with the idle target group. It can send test traffic through a test listener and run Lambda hooks, for example BeforeAllowTraffic, to smoke test. Then it shifts the production listener to the new target group, either all at once, in linear steps like ten percent every minute, or as a canary with a small slice first. CloudWatch alarms monitored during the shift can trigger an automatic rollback by sending traffic back to the original task set, which stays running for a configurable wait time before termination. The AppSpec file defines the task definition, container and port. This gives fast, low-risk releases without in-place changes.
f: What does the termination wait time do?
How would you do database migrations with blue/green?

q: A Lambda function in a VPC times out when calling RDS or an external API. How do you debug it?
p: Check the function's subnets, security groups and routes. Reaching RDS needs a security group rule from the function to the database port. Reaching the internet needs a NAT Gateway, since Lambda in a VPC has no public IP. Also check the timeout and connection reuse.
tip: Timeouts, rather than refusals, usually mean a dropped packet: missing route, security group or NACL.
a: I begin with the symptom. A connection that hangs until the timeout usually means packets are silently dropped, while an immediate error suggests a refusal or wrong credentials. First I look at the function's VPC configuration: which subnets and security groups it uses. For RDS, the database security group must allow the function's security group on the database port, and the subnets must be able to route to it. For an external API, a Lambda in a private subnet needs a route through a NAT Gateway, or a VPC endpoint if the target is an AWS service, because it does not get a public address. I also check network ACLs, DNS resolution, and whether the function timeout is shorter than the downstream call. For databases I look at connection exhaustion and use RDS Proxy, and I reuse connections across invocations. Reachability Analyzer is helpful for confirming the path.
f: How does Reachability Analyzer help?
Why is NAT needed for outbound internet from a VPC Lambda?

q: An ALB target group shows targets as unhealthy. How do you find out why?
p: Read the health check reason code, then verify the path, port and success codes match what the app serves, the security group allows the ALB to reach the target, the app is listening, and timeouts and thresholds are realistic.
tip: The reason field, such as Target.Timeout or Target.ResponseCodeMismatch, tells you which layer to look at.
a: The describe target health output includes a reason code that points to the layer. Target.Timeout means the health check could not connect, often because the target security group does not allow the load balancer's security group on the traffic or health check port, a network ACL blocks it, or the app is not listening. Target.ResponseCodeMismatch means the app responded but with a code that is not in the configured matcher, like a redirect or an authentication error on the health path. Target.FailedHealthChecks can be a slow response or a flapping app. I test from within the VPC using curl against the exact path and port, confirm the container port mapping and bind address, and check the app logs. Then I tune the interval, thresholds and timeout, and use a lightweight health endpoint that checks readiness without hitting heavy dependencies.
f: What path should a health check use?
How does ALB health differ from ASG health?

q: New EKS worker nodes launch but never join the cluster. What do you check?
p: Verify the node IAM role is mapped through an access entry or aws-auth, the bootstrap script and cluster name are correct, the node can reach the API endpoint and required AWS endpoints, security groups allow control plane traffic, and the CNI and kubelet start.
cmds: kubectl get cm aws-auth -n kube-system -o yaml
tip: Check the console output or system log first. Bootstrap errors usually appear there in plain text.
a: I start on the instance with the console output or, if I can connect via Session Manager, the cloud-init and kubelet logs. Common causes are these. The node's IAM role is not authorised in the cluster, which means a missing access entry or aws-auth mapping, so the kubelet gets unauthorized errors. The bootstrap parameters are wrong, such as a wrong cluster name or endpoint, or a custom AMI missing the bootstrap. Networking problems stop the node reaching the API server: private endpoint only without a route, security groups missing the cluster security group rules, or no access to ECR, S3 and STS through NAT or endpoints. The VPC CNI may not be able to assign IPs, leaving the node NotReady. I fix the specific gap, then terminate and let the group replace the node. To avoid this, I use managed node groups and test launch template changes in a non-production cluster.
f: What replaced aws-auth ConfigMap?
Why would a node be NotReady after joining?

q: A pod using IRSA gets 'WebIdentityErr' or AccessDenied from STS. What is wrong?
p: Check that the service account annotation and the pod's token projection exist, the OIDC provider is registered in IAM, and the role trust policy's sub and aud conditions exactly match the namespace and service account name.
tip: The pod must be restarted after annotating the service account, because the token is injected at pod creation.
a: The error means STS refused to exchange the pod's token for role credentials. I check from the pod outward. First, are the AWS role ARN and web identity token file environment variables present in the pod? If not, the service account annotation is missing or the pod was created before it was added, so it needs a restart. Next, I compare the cluster's OIDC issuer URL with the OIDC provider registered in IAM, since a mismatch or a deleted provider breaks everything. Then I read the role's trust policy: the principal must be that provider, the audience should be sts.amazonaws.com, and the subject condition must exactly match system:serviceaccount:namespace:name. Typos in the namespace or name are very common. Finally, I make sure the SDK in the image is recent enough to support web identity. I now prefer EKS Pod Identity for simpler trust.
f: What does the sub condition look like?
Why must the pod restart after annotation?

q: An EC2 instance fails a system or instance status check. What do you do?
p: System check failure points to AWS hardware or host, so stop and start the instance to move it to new hardware. Instance check failure points to the OS: boot problems, full disk, kernel panic, or bad network config. Use console output and screenshot, or attach the volume to a rescue instance.
cmds: aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-1 && aws ec2 start-instances --instance-ids i-1
tip: Remember reboot keeps the host, but stop then start usually migrates the instance. Instance store data is lost on stop.
a: I look at which status check is failing. A system status check failure means a problem with the underlying AWS infrastructure, such as host hardware or network connectivity. Stopping and starting the instance, not just rebooting, normally moves it to healthy hardware, and I can set a CloudWatch alarm with an auto-recover action for this. An instance status check failure means the operating system is not responding correctly, which could be a bad fstab, a full root volume, a kernel panic, broken network configuration or exhausted memory. I read the system log and screenshot from the console, and if I cannot log in, I stop the instance, detach the root volume, attach it to a rescue instance, fix the files, and reattach. For an Auto Scaling group I let health checks replace the instance, but still investigate the cause, because data on instance store volumes disappears.
f: Reboot versus stop and start?
How do you set up auto-recovery?

q: A VPC peering connection is active but instances cannot reach each other. What do you check?
p: Both VPCs need route table entries pointing the other CIDR to the peering connection, security groups and NACLs must allow the traffic, CIDRs must not overlap, and peering is not transitive. DNS resolution across peering must be enabled if you use private names.
tip: Reachability Analyzer shows exactly which hop blocks the path.
a: An active peering connection only creates the link. Nothing flows until the routes exist. So I check that the route table of each subnet in both VPCs has a route for the other VPC's CIDR with the peering connection as the target. Overlapping CIDRs make peering impossible or ambiguous, so I confirm they are distinct. Then I verify security groups, which can reference peer security groups in the same region, and network ACLs allow the ports in both directions. Peering is not transitive, so traffic cannot pass through a third VPC or through a VPN attached to one side, in which case I would use Transit Gateway. If connections work by IP but names fail, I enable DNS resolution over the peering for both sides. I use VPC Reachability Analyzer to verify the path, and then automate routes in infrastructure as code so they are not forgotten.
f: Why does peering not allow transit?
When would you move to Transit Gateway?

q: Private hosted zone names resolve in one VPC but not another. How do you fix it?
p: A private hosted zone only answers queries from VPCs associated with it. Associate the other VPC, which for cross-account VPCs needs an authorization and association call, and make sure enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames are on.
tip: For cross-account, first run create-vpc-association-authorization in the zone's account, then associate from the VPC's account.
a: A private hosted zone is attached to specific VPCs and only those VPCs' resolvers can answer for it. So the first step is to list the zones associated with the failing VPC. If the zone is missing, I associate the VPC with the hosted zone. When the zone and the VPC are in different accounts, the zone owner creates an association authorization and then the VPC owner completes the association. I also confirm that DNS support and DNS hostnames are enabled on the VPC, otherwise the VPC resolver does not work for private zones. For many VPCs, I would use Route 53 Resolver rules or share the zone via Resource Access Manager or Route 53 Profiles, rather than associating one by one. If hybrid names are involved, I check that resolver endpoints and forwarding rules are in place. Finally, I test with dig against the VPC resolver address.
f: What is the VPC resolver address?
How do Route 53 Profiles simplify this?

q: A CloudFormation stack is stuck in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED. How do you recover?
p: Find the resource that failed to roll back in the stack events, fix the cause such as a manually changed or deleted resource, then use ContinueUpdateRollback, optionally skipping the stuck resources. Afterwards, address drift and retry the update.
tip: Skipping a resource leaves it out of sync, so you must reconcile it manually afterwards.
a: This state means CloudFormation tried to roll back a failed update, but could not restore one of the resources. I read the stack events to find the first failure and the specific reason. Typical causes are someone manually deleting or modifying a resource the rollback needs, an IAM permission missing for the stack's role, a resource dependency, or a service limit. I fix the underlying problem, for example recreating the deleted item or granting the role permission, and then call continue update rollback. If a resource cannot be restored, I can tell CloudFormation to skip it, which moves the stack to a stable state but leaves that resource out of sync, so I then check drift and repair it. As prevention, I stop manual changes with guardrails, use change sets to review updates, set rollback triggers, and use stack policies for critical resources.
f: What is a change set?
How does drift detection work?

q: An ECS deployment keeps failing and rolling back because new tasks fail health checks. How do you get to the cause?
p: Look at the service events and stopped task reasons, then the container logs and exit code. Common causes are a wrong container port or health check path, missing secrets or environment, a slow startup that needs a grace period, and insufficient memory.
tip: Set healthCheckGracePeriodSeconds for slow-starting apps so the load balancer does not kill them during startup.
a: The service events and the stopped task details usually tell the story. A stopped reason such as Task failed ELB health checks means the app started but was not answering correctly, while an exit code of one thirty-seven suggests an out-of-memory kill and two-fifty-five or one points to an application crash. I read the container logs for startup errors, such as missing environment variables, secrets that the execution role cannot read, or a database that cannot be reached. I then verify the port mapping, the target group health check path and matcher, and that the security groups allow the load balancer. For slow starters I add a health check grace period and a longer deregistration timing. Circuit breaker rollback is helpful because it returns to the last good version automatically, but I always fix the underlying issue and test the task definition in a staging service first.
f: What is the ECS deployment circuit breaker?
What does exit code 137 mean?

q: The root EBS volume is almost full on a production instance. How do you expand it without downtime?
p: Modify the volume size online, then grow the partition and filesystem inside the OS, with growpart and resize2fs or xfs_growfs. You can modify once every six hours per volume. Take a snapshot first, and find what filled the disk.
tip: Check inodes with df -i as well. A disk can be full of tiny files while showing free space.
a: First, I take a snapshot for safety. Then I use the volume modification API to increase the size, which works online for current generation instances. I wait for the modification to reach the optimizing state, which is enough for use. Inside the instance I grow the partition with growpart, then extend the filesystem using resize2fs for ext4 or xfs_growfs for XFS. There is a cooldown of about six hours before the same volume can be modified again, so I choose a size with headroom. Expanding is a stopgap, so I find why it filled: logs without rotation, old Docker images, core dumps or temp files, using du and checking deleted files still held open with lsof. I fix log rotation, move data to a separate volume, and set a CloudWatch alarm on disk usage with the agent, because disk metrics are not collected by default.
f: Why check inodes?
Can you shrink an EBS volume?

q: Important objects were deleted from an S3 bucket. How do you recover them, and how do you prevent a repeat?
p: If versioning was on, the delete only added a delete marker, so remove the marker or copy the earlier version back. Without versioning, check replication targets, backups, or AWS Backup. Prevent with versioning, MFA delete, Object Lock and restrictive policies.
tip: Deleting a specific version is permanent, so only users who truly need it should have s3:DeleteObjectVersion.
a: My action depends on whether versioning was enabled. With versioning, a normal delete just places a delete marker on top, so I list the versions and either delete the marker or copy the previous version to become current again, which I can script for many keys. If a specific version was deleted, it is gone, so I check cross-region or same-region replication targets, other backups, AWS Backup for S3, or application-level copies. I also check CloudTrail data events, if enabled, to learn who deleted what and why. To prevent repeats, I enable versioning on important buckets, add lifecycle rules for noncurrent versions, consider Object Lock in compliance or governance mode for critical data, require MFA delete for permanent deletions, restrict delete permissions, and replicate to a separate account. Regular restore drills prove it works.
f: What does Object Lock compliance mode guarantee?
How do you restore millions of objects?

q: After an RDS Multi-AZ failover, the application kept failing for several minutes. Why, and how do you fix it?
p: The endpoint DNS changes to the new primary, but apps cache DNS or hold dead connections. Use short DNS TTL honoured by the runtime, connection validation and retry with backoff, pool limits, and RDS Proxy to shield clients.
tip: Test failover on purpose in staging. It is the only way to know your connection handling works.
a: During failover RDS promotes the standby and updates the DNS record of the endpoint, which typically takes one to two minutes, and existing connections drop. Applications fail longer than that when they cache the old IP address, for example a JVM with an infinite DNS cache TTL, or keep broken pooled connections and do not validate them. Fixing it involves several steps. I make sure the runtime respects a short DNS TTL, configure the connection pool to test connections and evict broken ones, and add retries with exponential backoff and jitter for transient errors. I set sensible connect and read timeouts so threads do not hang. RDS Proxy can mask much of the failover by keeping client connections open. I schedule a forced failover in staging regularly, observe how the app behaves, and document the expected recovery time in the runbook and alerts.
f: What is JVM networkaddress.cache.ttl?
How does RDS Proxy reduce failover impact?

q: A DynamoDB table is throttling even though consumed capacity is below the provisioned limit. What is happening?
p: A hot partition. Traffic concentrated on a few partition keys exceeds the per-partition limits, about 1,000 writes and 3,000 reads per second. Fix the key design with higher-cardinality keys, write sharding, caching, or on-demand mode, and check for hot GSIs.
cmds: aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/DynamoDB --metric-name WriteThrottleEvents --dimensions Name=TableName,Value=orders --start-time 2026-10-20T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-10-21T00:00:00Z --period 300 --statistics Sum
tip: Contributor Insights shows the most accessed partition keys directly, so enable it during diagnosis.
a: Capacity is spread across partitions, and each partition has its own throughput ceiling. If requests concentrate on a small set of keys, such as a date, a popular product or a status value, a single partition can throttle while the table total still looks low. I confirm by looking at throttle metrics and enabling CloudWatch Contributor Insights to see the hottest keys. Fixes depend on the pattern. I redesign the partition key for higher cardinality, or add a shard suffix to spread writes and aggregate on read. For read-heavy hot items, I add DAX or an application cache. Adaptive capacity helps with some imbalance, but it is not a substitute for good key design. A global secondary index can also throttle the base table if its own key is hot, so I check those. On-demand mode removes capacity planning but does not remove partition limits.
f: What is write sharding?
How does adaptive capacity help?

q: Aurora read replicas show growing replica lag. How do you diagnose it?
p: Aurora replicas share storage, so lag is normally milliseconds. Growing lag usually means heavy write volume, long-running queries on the replica blocking replay, an undersized replica, or a large transaction. Check AuroraReplicaLag, CPU, and Performance Insights.
cmds: aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/RDS --metric-name AuroraReplicaLag --dimensions Name=DBInstanceIdentifier,Value=prod-ro1 --start-time 2026-10-21T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-10-21T06:00:00Z --period 60 --statistics Maximum
SELECT pid, now() - query_start AS dur, query FROM pg_stat_activity ORDER BY dur DESC LIMIT 5;
tip: In Aurora, a replica that is smaller than the writer can struggle to apply changes during heavy write bursts.
a: Unlike classic RDS replicas, Aurora replicas read from the same distributed storage as the writer, so lag is typically small and relates to the replica refreshing its in-memory cache and page versions. If lag grows I first look at the writer: a burst of heavy writes, bulk loads or very large transactions create lots of changes for the replicas to apply. Then I check the replica itself: CPU or memory pressure, an instance class much smaller than the writer, and long-running queries that conflict with replay, which can delay or cancel work. Performance Insights shows the waits and top SQL. Fixes include breaking up large batch writes, right-sizing replicas, killing or optimising slow reporting queries, routing heavy analytics to a dedicated replica, and making the application tolerant of slight staleness by sending read-after-write requests to the writer.
f: Which reads must go to the writer?
How do Aurora custom endpoints help?

q: The CloudWatch bill is suddenly very high. Where do you look and how do you cut it?
p: Break the CloudWatch charges down by usage type. Log ingestion and storage, custom metrics with high-cardinality dimensions, detailed monitoring, vended logs such as VPC Flow Logs, and API polling are the usual drivers.
cmds: aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-10-01,End=2026-10-21 --granularity DAILY --metrics UnblendedCost --filter '{"Dimensions":{"Key":"SERVICE","Values":["AmazonCloudWatch"]}}' --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=USAGE_TYPE
tip: Setting a retention period on every log group is the cheapest quick win, because the default is to keep logs forever.
a: I start with Cost Explorer filtered to CloudWatch and grouped by usage type, which separates log ingestion, log storage, custom metrics, alarms and API requests. If ingestion dominates, I find the noisiest log groups using stored bytes and incoming bytes metrics, and typically see debug logging left on, a chatty library, or a retry storm. I lower log levels, sample noisy events, filter before shipping, and set retention on every group, with older data archived to S3. If custom metrics are the issue, high-cardinality dimensions such as user ID or request ID create enormous numbers of metrics, so I remove those dimensions or use embedded metric format with limited dimensions. VPC Flow Logs can go to S3 instead, which is cheaper. Finally I add a budget alert and anomaly detection on CloudWatch spend.
f: Why is cardinality costly for metrics?
When would you ship logs to S3 instead?

q: Savings Plan coverage dropped after migrating workloads to Fargate and Graviton. What happened and what do you do?
p: Instance-specific commitments, like EC2 Instance Savings Plans or RIs, do not cover Fargate, and changing architecture can leave commitments unused while new usage is billed on-demand. Review coverage and utilisation, and prefer Compute Savings Plans.
tip: Plan commitments around the target architecture, and keep some baseline uncommitted while migrations are in flight.
a: I compare utilisation and coverage. Utilisation shows how much of what we committed is actually being used, and coverage shows how much of our eligible spend is covered. After the migration, an EC2 Instance Savings Plan tied to old instance families may sit unused, because those instances were retired, while Fargate and Graviton usage is billed at on-demand rates. A Compute Savings Plan would have followed the workload across EC2, Fargate and Lambda and across families, including Graviton. Remedies: if the unused commitment is large, I can move workloads back temporarily, use it up where possible, wait for expiry and avoid renewal. For new usage I buy a Compute Savings Plan sized to the new stable baseline. Going forward, I time commitment purchases after migrations settle, buy in smaller steps, and review monthly with finance.
f: Can Savings Plans be cancelled?
Why keep some baseline uncommitted?

q: Lambda throttling in one function is starving other functions in the account. How do you contain it?
p: All functions in a region share the account concurrency limit. Set reserved concurrency on important functions to guarantee capacity and on noisy ones to cap them, add queues to smooth bursts, request a quota increase, and alarm on throttles.
cmds: aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/Lambda --metric-name Throttles --dimensions Name=FunctionName,Value=ingest --start-time 2026-10-21T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-10-21T06:00:00Z --period 60 --statistics Sum
tip: Reserved concurrency is both a guarantee and a hard cap for that function, so size it carefully.
a: Lambda has a regional account limit on concurrent executions, shared by all functions unless reserved. A flood of invocations in one function, such as a retry storm or a large batch from S3 or SQS, can consume that pool and cause throttling for unrelated, more important functions. To contain it, I set reserved concurrency on the critical functions, which guarantees them capacity, and on the noisy one to cap how much it can take, which also protects downstream databases. For bursty producers I introduce an SQS queue between them and the function, with a batch size and maximum concurrency on the event source mapping, so the load is smoothed rather than spiking. I request a higher account limit when justified, and set alarms on the Throttles and ConcurrentExecutions metrics. For latency sensitive functions I can add provisioned concurrency.
f: Reserved versus provisioned concurrency?
How do you cap SQS-triggered concurrency?

q: Instances in an Auto Scaling group keep terminating and relaunching in a loop. How do you stop it and find the cause?
p: Usually the health check fails right after launch, from slow bootstrap, a wrong health check path, or an ELB check starting before the app is up. Look at scaling activity history, set a health check grace period, and test the launch template in isolation.
tip: Suspending the Terminate process lets you keep one failing instance alive to inspect, but resume it afterwards.
a: The scaling activity history gives the termination reason, for example failed ELB health checks or an EC2 status check failure. The common cause is that new instances are marked unhealthy before the application is ready, because bootstrap takes longer than the health check grace period, or the health check path or port is wrong, or a user data script fails. To investigate I temporarily suspend the terminate process, or put an instance in standby, so I can log in and read cloud-init and application logs. I test the launch template alone by launching a single instance. Fixes include extending the grace period, baking the AMI to cut boot time, correcting the health check, and fixing the failing script, then resuming the processes. I also use lifecycle hooks to wait for readiness, and set alarms on the unhealthy host count so such loops are noticed quickly.
f: What does standby do?
Why bake AMIs instead of long user data scripts?

q: ECS tasks fail with CannotPullContainerError. How do you diagnose it?
p: The task cannot fetch its image. Check the image name and tag, the execution role's ECR permissions, network path to ECR and S3 (NAT or endpoints) for private subnets, registry rate limits, and available disk or image size.
cmds: aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin <acct>.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com
tip: Private Fargate tasks need ecr.api, ecr.dkr and the S3 gateway endpoint, or a NAT Gateway.
a: The stopped reason usually states the cause. If it says the image was not found, I check the repository, tag and region, since a typo or a tag that was never pushed is common. If it says access denied or no basic auth credentials, the task execution role lacks ECR permissions such as GetAuthorizationToken and BatchGetImage, or the repository policy blocks a cross-account pull. If it times out, the network path is the problem: in private subnets tasks need a route through a NAT Gateway or the VPC endpoints for ECR API, ECR Docker and the S3 gateway endpoint, because layers are stored in S3, and security groups must allow outbound HTTPS. For images from Docker Hub, rate limiting can happen, so I mirror them into ECR or use pull-through cache. Very large images also slow starts, so I slim them.
f: Why is an S3 endpoint needed for ECR?
What is an ECR pull-through cache?

q: An EKS control plane upgrade is blocked or add-ons break afterwards. How do you plan to avoid that?
p: Check upgrade insights for deprecated APIs, confirm add-on and node versions are compatible, upgrade one minor version at a time, upgrade add-ons and managed node groups after the control plane, and use PodDisruptionBudgets that allow drains.
tip: A PDB with maxUnavailable zero and a single replica makes node drains hang forever, so audit PDBs before the upgrade.
a: Preparation matters more than the upgrade command. I run upgrade readiness insights and tools like Pluto to find deprecated or removed APIs in the cluster and in Git. I read the release notes for the target version, confirm versions of the VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, CSI drivers, ingress controllers and any operators support it, and test the whole thing in a non-production cluster. The control plane upgrades first, one minor version at a time, and EKS keeps it available. Then I update the add-ons, and roll the node groups, preferably with surge nodes so capacity remains. Drains can hang because of strict PodDisruptionBudgets, so I check those beforehand, and ensure workloads have more than one replica. I take backups of state like etcd-equivalent manifests, plan a maintenance window, and keep a rollback plan of building a new node group on the previous version.
f: Why can PDBs block node drains?
What is a blue/green cluster upgrade?

q: A CloudWatch alarm sits in INSUFFICIENT_DATA and never fires during a real outage. What is wrong?
p: The alarm is not receiving data points, or the missing-data treatment hides the problem. A crashed service emits no metrics, so default behaviour stays in insufficient data. Set treat missing data to breaching, or alarm on a heartbeat or the absence of metrics.
cmds: aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name api-heartbeat --metric-name RequestCount --namespace AWS/ApplicationELB --statistic Sum --period 60 --evaluation-periods 5 --threshold 1 --comparison-operator LessThanThreshold --treat-missing-data breaching
tip: Alerting on error counts alone fails when the service is completely down, so also alarm on lack of traffic.
a: If the thing you monitor stops sending metrics, an error-count alarm has nothing to evaluate, so it goes to insufficient data instead of alarm. During a real outage, when the service is down and not emitting errors or traffic, the alarm stays quiet. I first check the alarm configuration: the metric name, namespace and dimensions must exactly match the data actually published, since a mismatch gives permanent insufficient data. Then I choose how to treat missing data. For availability signals, I treat missing as breaching, so no data means a problem, whereas for sparse metrics I treat it as not breaching. I also add alarms for the absence of expected traffic, for example request count below one for five minutes, use synthetic canaries that test the endpoint from outside, and a heartbeat metric. Alarms should be tested by deliberately causing failures in staging.
f: What are CloudWatch Synthetics canaries?
When do you treat missing data as not breaching?

q: A Lambda or ECS service runs but no logs appear in CloudWatch. What do you check?
p: Check the role has logs:CreateLogStream and PutLogEvents, the log group exists or can be created, the task definition log driver and options are right, network access to the logs endpoint exists from private subnets, and the app actually writes to stdout.
tip: For ECS, the execution role does log delivery, not the task role.
a: I work through the path logs take. Does the application write to standard output or standard error, rather than to a file inside the container? For Lambda, the execution role needs permission to create the log group and streams and put events, and a deleted log group or a missing permission is a frequent cause. For ECS, the task definition needs a log configuration using the awslogs driver or FireLens, with the right group, region and stream prefix, and the task execution role needs logs permissions. In private subnets there must be a route to CloudWatch Logs through NAT or a VPC endpoint. I also check whether a log group retention or resource policy exists, whether log volume is hitting service throttles, and if a sidecar log router is failing. I confirm using simulate-principal-policy and the agent or router logs, then fix and redeploy.

q: Assuming a role across accounts fails with 'not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRole'. How do you fix it?
p: Cross-account access needs two sides: the caller's identity policy allows sts:AssumeRole on the target role, and the target role's trust policy names the caller's account or principal. Check conditions such as ExternalId, MFA, and SCPs.
tip: If the trust policy names an account root, the caller still needs its own explicit allow. Both sides must agree.
a: Role assumption across accounts requires agreement from both sides. In the target account, the role's trust policy must list the caller as a trusted principal: the account, a specific role, or user. In the source account, the calling identity needs an identity policy that allows sts:AssumeRole on that role's ARN, unless the trust policy names the exact principal and it is in the same account. When it fails, I read the trust policy for typos in account IDs and role names, and conditions like ExternalId, MFA required, source IP, or an organization ID that the request does not satisfy. I also check for permission boundaries and service control policies that deny assume role, and whether the session is a role chain, which has a one hour limit. I use the policy simulator and CloudTrail events to see the exact denial reason, then correct whichever side is missing and retest.

q: A dead-letter queue is filling up with messages. How do you investigate and drain it safely?
p: Inspect messages and attributes to find why processing failed: poison payloads, bugs, downstream outages, or visibility timeout too short. Fix the cause, then redrive messages back to the source queue, and alarm on queue depth and age.
tip: Only redrive after the bug is fixed, or the messages will just return to the DLQ and burn retries.
a: A growing dead-letter queue means messages exceeded the maximum receive count on the source queue. First I sample a few messages and their attributes, and correlate with consumer logs by message ID, to find the failure pattern. It could be malformed payloads that will never succeed, a code bug on a specific input, a downstream dependency that was down, or a visibility timeout shorter than the processing time, which makes messages reappear mid-processing and eventually move. For poison messages I fix or discard them with a record of what happened. For transient failures, I fix the dependency, deploy any code fix, and then use the redrive feature to move messages back to the source queue, possibly with a controlled rate. I make consumers idempotent, set an alarm on DLQ visible messages and oldest message age, and keep a runbook for it.
